```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Purpose

This report demonstrates the type of R / R Markdown pipeline I build and
maintain for the Mathematics and R Laboratory course I teach: it reads a
raw exercise dataset, checks and cleans it, computes descriptive
statistics, and produces visualisations, all compiled automatically into a
single reproducible document.

The dataset used here is **synthetic** (see `generate_data.R`): no real
student data is included in this repository.

## 1. Reading the raw data

```{r read-data}
raw <- read.csv("data/lab_exercise_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
str(raw)
```

## 2. Data quality checks and cleaning

Before any analysis, I check for missing values and implausible entries
(e.g. scores outside the valid 0-30 range), which routinely occur in raw
exercise/exam datasets.

```{r quality-checks}
missing_summary <- colSums(is.na(raw))
missing_summary

out_of_range <- raw %>%
  filter(written_score < 0 | written_score > 30 | is.na(written_score))
out_of_range
```

```{r cleaning}
clean <- raw %>%
  filter(!is.na(attendance_pct)) %>%
  mutate(
    written_score = ifelse(written_score < 0 | written_score > 30,
                            NA, written_score)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(written_score))

cat("Rows before cleaning:", nrow(raw), "\n")
cat("Rows after cleaning: ", nrow(clean), "\n")
```

## 3. Aggregation

Cross-checking written and lab scores by cohort, similar to how grades are
aggregated and cross-checked across written and lab-based assessments for
the examination committee.

```{r aggregation}
summary_by_cohort <- clean %>%
  group_by(cohort) %>%
  summarise(
    n              = n(),
    mean_written   = round(mean(written_score), 2),
    mean_lab       = round(mean(lab_score), 2),
    sd_written     = round(sd(written_score), 2),
    median_written = median(written_score)
  )

summary_by_cohort
```

## 4. Descriptive statistics

```{r descriptives}
summary(clean[, c("hours_studied", "attendance_pct",
                   "written_score", "lab_score")])
```

## 5. Visualisation

```{r plot-histogram, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(clean, aes(x = written_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Written Exam Scores",
       x = "Score", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r plot-boxplot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(clean, aes(x = cohort, y = lab_score, fill = cohort)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Lab Scores by Cohort",
       x = "Cohort", y = "Lab score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r plot-scatter, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(clean, aes(x = hours_studied, y = written_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#4C72B0") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Hours Studied vs Written Score",
       x = "Hours studied", y = "Written score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 6. A simple regression check

As a further illustration of the statistical-computing exercises used in
the lab, a simple linear model relating hours studied to written score:

```{r regression}
model <- lm(written_score ~ hours_studied + attendance_pct, data = clean)
summary(model)
```

## Notes

This document is knit directly from the underlying CSV: updating
`data/lab_exercise_data.csv` (or re-running `generate_data.R`) and
re-knitting reproduces the full report -- the same reproducible workflow
used for the lab sessions.
